slide_text: Visualizing Data using t-SNE

Laurens van der Maaten¹  ·  Geoffrey Hinton²
¹ Tilburg University     ² University of Toronto
Introduction

• Which neighbors stay together when thousands of dimensions become two?
• A two-dimensional scatterplot offers less room than the original space.
• Crowding can hide groups or separate nearby samples.
• The goal is to preserve local neighborhoods and reveal clusters at multiple scales.
• A crowded map can hide groups present in the input.
Stochastic Neighbor Embedding

• SNE turns distances into probabilities of choosing a neighbor.
• Each sample defines a distribution over the other samples.
• Fit the map by minimizing the KL divergence between the input and map distributions.
• Separating a likely input neighbor incurs a large penalty.
• SNE estimates neighbor probabilities in the input and the map.
t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding
Symmetric SNE

• Symmetric SNE assigns each pair one joint similarity.
• Combine the two conditional probabilities so both directions contribute.
• This objective gives each observation a role and simplifies the gradient used to move map points.
The Crowding Problem

• In high dimensions, many points can be moderately close to the same observation.
• A plane has less room at comparable distances.
• Preserving all those neighbor distances can crowd points toward the center of the map.
Mismatched Tails can Compensate for Mismatched Dimensiona…

• Gaussian similarities describe neighbors in the input space.
• The map uses a Student t distribution with one degree of freedom.
• Its heavy tails give moderately dissimilar points room to separate.
Optimization Methods for t-SNE

• Gradient descent moves points using momentum and adaptive learning rates.
• Early exaggeration temporarily strengthens attractions among neighbors.
• Groups form while they can still move past one another.
Experiments
Data Sets

• MNIST uses 6,000 handwritten digits sampled from 60,000 images.
• Olivetti contains 400 face images, ten per person.
Experimental Setup

• Use the same images.
• Perplexity sets neighborhood size.
Results

• Many handwritten digit classes form separate neighborhoods.
• The map also groups variations in writing style within a class.
• Many handwritten digit classes form distinct neighborhoods.

• Face images test whether identity remains visible across appearances.
• Object views test whether gradual rotation remains traceable.
• Compare t-SNE with Sammon mapping, Isomap and LLE.
Applying t-SNE to Large Data Sets

• Random walks use every observation to connect selected landmarks.
• All 60,000 MNIST images inform the map of 6,000 landmarks.
• Ten-fold 1-NN error: 5.13% in 2D versus 5.75% in 784D.
• Landmarks reduce how many coordinates must be optimized.
• On a graph of all observations, random walks estimate similarities between these landmarks.
Discussion
Comparison with Related Techniques

• The penalty is asymmetric: missing a close input neighbor matters more.
• Inspect neighborhoods before interpreting distances across clusters.
• The asymmetric divergence gives priority to nearby input points that are distant in the map.
Weaknesses

• The formulation targets two- and three-dimensional visualization.
• High intrinsic dimensionality can obscure meaningful neighborhoods.
• Different initializations may reach different local optima.
• t-SNE targets visualization in two or three dimensions.
Conclusions

• Heavy-tailed map similarities reduce crowding.
• The original algorithm uses quadratic time and memory.
• Random-walk landmarks extend visualization to larger collections.
• Heavy-tailed map probabilities alleviate crowding and reveal local neighborhoods and clusters at multiple scales.
• Standard t-SNE takes quadratic time and memory.
• Random-walk landmarks extend its use to larger collections.
